title: Queue-Based Load Leveling

validation.research: Eight primary references: Microsoft catalogs Queue-Based Load Leveling; AWS documents backlog debt, recovery and message-age monitoring; RabbitMQ separates publisher confirms from consumer acknowledgment and documents prefetch scope; SQS visibility and at-least-once documents establish pending deletion, redelivery and duplicates; RFC 9110 defines acceptance before completion and status monitoring; Python documents deque operations; AWS Elastic Load Balancing documentation distinguishes distribution across targets from buffering through time. British load levelling and the unhyphenated spelling are search aliases. No existing article is equivalent: Producer-Consumer describes the participants; Backpressure regulates admission feedback; Bulkhead isolates capacity allowances; Idempotent Receiver handles repeated effects. The report scenario, chosen capacities, discrete phase convention, trace, code and diagrams are original teaching material.

runnable_example.verification: Actual article fences run unchanged on Python 3.11+. Exact header/four rows match every illustrated value. Strict tuple/integer validation rejects Boolean, fractional, negative and malformed inputs. Empty/idle input, admission-before-drain phase, explicit capacity refusal, trillion-count burst with only two retained identities, zero-service outage, finite horizon/residual work and appended idle recovery are checked. The sustained (4,4,4,4) case rejects four and leaves four waiting. Observation wraps the actual deque without replacing simulation logic: retained jobs remain FIFO, no maxlen eviction occurs, waiting stays within capacity, and removals match counted completions. 7500 finite traces verify independent per-phase and total conservation, bounded waiting, admission and service budget. This is a unit-cost virtual-time model, not a live limiter or broker; persistence, concurrent execution, retries, acknowledgments, byte accounting, duplicate-safe effects and actual external success are not simulated.

example_limits: Original report-generation scenario and finite Python 3.11+ virtual-time FIFO simulation. One tick is one second: validate the finite tuple and integer budgets, admit up to the waiting capacity at tick start, explicitly count rejected arrivals, complete up to a unit-job service budget, and sample waiting at tick end. The (6,2,0,0) trace accepts eight, completes two per tick and finishes empty. The (4,4,4,4) overload trace rejects four and leaves four waiting. A zero budget models no service over the supplied horizon. No execution spans ticks. The deque holds only accepted job identities; a finite input tuple and returned trace use additional memory. No durable broker, real timer or rate-limiter implementation, concurrent workers, acknowledgments, retries, payload bytes or external effects are simulated. Real production rate/concurrency control, durable confirmation, duplicate-safe effects, retained input/status ownership and shutdown must be supplied separately. Established Queue-Based Load Leveling title; British spelling alias and unhyphenated search alias. New canonical article; existing Producer-Consumer, Backpressure, Bulkhead and Idempotent Receiver remain intact. Tests independently verify conservation, strict validation, explicit refusal, FIFO removal, budget and waiting bounds over 7500 finite traces. The zero-service case models an outage, not a running worker or broker failure. Simulation completion assumes unit-cost success; no real-time pacing, durability, concurrent acknowledgment, retry or business effect is inferred.
